title: the Arthashastra's opening
tomorrow: crowned at last. who does a new king still have to listen to?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Arthashastra's opening named danda, the rod, and the law of the fish: without it, the big fish eat the small. Today, how hard the rod should strike.

A referee who whistles every tiny bump gets booed off the field. One who whistles nothing loses the game to elbows. The crowd ends up trusting the one who calls it straight. Same whistle, three results. The Arthashastra makes that point about a king's rod, right after it says why the rod is needed. So, one question today: how hard should power strike?
screen: `SAME WHISTLE, THREE REFEREES.` → `HOW HARD SHOULD POWER STRIKE?`

segments.voice: The text sets out three rulers. One strikes too hard, and people are terrified of him. One is too mild, and people despise him. The third uses the rod justly, after thinking it through, and he is honored. Then the test: used with care, the rod leaves people free for the aims of life: doing right, making a living, enjoying life. Used out of desire, anger or ignorance, it enrages even hermits in the forest, who own nothing. Buddhists have a verse that looks at the same rod from the other end, from the one it falls on. In the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death." The Pali word for punishment there is danda, the same rod. And the verse goes on, in paraphrase: remember that others are like you, and do not kill or cause killing. Here's what the two share. Neither weighs the rod by the arm that swings it. Both weigh it by the person who feels it, and by a fear everyone shares. And the honest difference: the Arthashastra keeps the rod in the king's hand and asks him to use it justly. The Dhammapada verse speaks to each person, and asks them not to strike at all.
screen: `TOO HARD: FEARED. TOO MILD: DESPISED.` · `JUST, AND THOUGHT THROUGH: HONORED.` · `ALL TREMBLE AT THE ROD.` · `ONE KEEPS THE ROD; ONE PUTS IT DOWN.` · then, large: `WEIGHED BY THE ONE WHO FEELS IT.`

segments.voice: Notice your hands and your jaw. If they're gripping, let them soften a little; if they've gone slack, gather them back to a gentle hold. Rest in that middle grip for the sit, not too hard, not too soft.
The Arthashastra's opening: the measured rod, not too harsh and not too mild, used so people can live well.
Keep this: the Arthashastra's opening, a rod weighed by the people who feel it. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're babysitting two kids, and one hits the other over a toy. by the measured rod, what's the consequence?
options: no screens for a week, so it never happens again.
a short break and a quick talk, then back to playing.
laugh it off. kids hit; nobody needs a consequence.
fork.reveal: too harsh breeds fear, too mild gets ignored. a just consequence, thought through, keeps both kids free to play. and the Dhammapada would add: the one hit felt the same fear you would.

original.note: Sanskrit danda, a rod or staff; the Pali daṇḍa in Dhammapada 129 is the same word.

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): Dhammapada 129, Max Müller 1881, quoted only for its first clause, 'All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death'; please check against the 1881 text (Sacred Books of the East vol. X). The rest of the verse is paraphrased ('remember that others are like you, and do not kill or cause killing'). The Pali 'sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa' uses daṇḍa; a Buddhist reviewer should confirm the framing 'the same rod'. Shared: both weigh the rod by the one who feels it. Honest difference: the Arthashastra keeps a just rod in the king's hand; the verse asks each person not to strike. No ranking.
The referee hook is modern framing only.
